enrichment.translation_en:
CYRANO (writing, aside—we hear him murmur from time to time):
  **I love you**…
enrichment.larger_context_summary: Cyrano is privately writing a letter to Roxane while awaiting a confidential meeting with her at Ragueneau’s pastry shop. He loves his cousin but, ashamed of his appearance, has not openly courted her; her request to meet has nevertheless raised his hopes. The letter lets him formulate what he cannot yet say directly under his own name. Soon afterward, Roxane reveals that she loves the handsome Christian and asks Cyrano to protect him, setting up Cyrano’s painful role as the hidden author of language used in another man’s courtship.
enrichment.interpretive_commentary: The wording is an unqualified assertion of Cyrano’s love, and the private act of composition strongly supports its sincerity: the audience knows that the feeling belongs to him even though the letter’s eventual communicative role is complicated. Its force is therefore primarily truth-presenting—an avowal—rather than performative. Although writing a love letter can affect a relationship and advance courtship, “I love you” does not itself promise future conduct, establish an obligation, or formally alter the relationship. Nor does the murmuring make it a reflexive emotional discharge: the stage direction depicts deliberate composition, with the words intermittently voiced as he writes. The dramatic interest lies in the split between genuine authorship and difficult delivery. Cyrano can state the truth in writing before he can safely declare it face to face, foreshadowing the play’s broader pattern of sincere feeling communicated indirectly or under another man’s identity.
